topic: When a good eval score lies

beats.vo: Ali built a grading assistant for his school, and every week its score climbed higher.

beats.vo: By the fourth week the score had gone from good to almost perfect.
Then a teacher told him the grades it was giving her class were plainly wrong.

beats.vo: The number said the assistant was getting better while the actual work was getting worse.

beats.vo: So Ali opened the set of examples he had been scoring against every single week.
beats.art: flat 2D vector illustration, clean geometric shapes, warm cream background, soft muted palette of teal, terracotta and sand, no text, no letters, no numbers, no labels, no signage, no writing of any kind. a young Pakistani man in his twenties, short black hair, warm brown skin, wearing a simple teal collared shirt and dark trousers seen from behind at a desk, looking at a grid of twenty small identical blank cards arranged neatly in front of him, plain cream room, no writing

beats.vo: It was the same twenty examples it had always been, and he had been tuning against them the whole time.

beats.vo: His assistant had not learned to grade well, it had learned those twenty answers.

topic: When an agent should stop and ask a human

research.topic: When an agent should stop and ask a human — deciding, before it acts, whether a step is safe to take alone or must be escalated
research.slo: Given a step an agent is about to take, the learner can decide whether the agent should proceed alone or stop and ask a human, by testing the step for reversibility, blast radius, and whether the agent's confidence about intent is high enough — and can encode that test as an explicit escalation rule instead of hoping the model behaves.
research.audience: Learners on the agentic-AI track who have already built an agent that uses tools and runs several steps on its own. They understand tool calls, loops, and prompts. They have not yet had to decide where an agent's authority ends, and they have never written an escalation rule.
key_points: The decision is per-STEP, not per-agent: the same agent can be fully autonomous on one action and required to stop on the next one in the same run.
Three tests decide it, in order: (1) Is it reversible? (2) How wide is the blast radius — one row or every row? (3) Does the agent actually know what the human wanted, or is it guessing intent?
Any single 'no' — irreversible, wide, or guessing — means stop and ask. Two 'yes' answers do not outvote one 'no'.
Asking is not failure and it is not weakness; the cost of one clarifying question is seconds, while the cost of a wrong irreversible action is hours of cleanup and lost trust.
The rule must live outside the model's judgement — as a checked condition in the agent's code around the tool, not as a polite sentence in the prompt saying 'ask if unsure'.
A good stop is a SPECIFIC question with the agent's proposed action attached, so the human answers yes/no in one breath instead of re-doing the reasoning.
NOTE — this video teaches only the STOP-OR-GO decision. How to design the approval interface, queue, or timeout behaviour is a separate concept and is deliberately left out.
research.ali_scenario: Ali has built a small support-inbox agent for Taleemabad. Every morning it reads the overnight teacher emails and tidies the ticket board. This morning there are 47 emails. The agent's job list for each one is: read it, tag it (Billing / App bug / Lesson content), reply with the matching template, and — if the teacher asks to leave — close the account. Ali watches it start at 9:02 a.m. Email 12 is from a teacher in Multan: 'The app keeps crashing on the Grade 4 lesson, I'm done with this, remove me.' The agent tags it App bug, sends the bug-report template, and then — reading 'remove me' — calls delete_account on her. One row. One irreversible call. Three years of her saved lesson plans gone at 9:04 a.m.
research.friction: Ali built the agent as one flat loop: for each email, do all four steps, no exceptions. He gave the model authority over the whole list because all four steps looked equally routine to him — they were all just 'handle an email'. So the agent applied the same confidence to sending a template as to deleting a teacher's account. It never paused on email 12, because nothing in the loop could pause. Ali only finds out at 11 a.m. when the teacher emails again asking where her lesson plans went, and he has no undo — deleted is deleted. Worse: he cannot tell Aroma how many of the other 46 emails got the same treatment without re-reading all of them.
research.fix: Ali stops treating the four steps as one block and runs each one through three questions before he gives the agent authority over it. Tagging: reversible (re-tag it), blast radius one ticket, intent clear from the text — GO. Sending a template: mostly reversible (you can follow up), one recipient, intent clear — GO. Deleting an account: NOT reversible, and 'I'm done with this, remove me' could mean 'delete my account' or 'stop emailing me' or just 'I'm furious' — he is guessing intent. STOP. So he wraps the delete tool in a real gate in code: if the action is on the irreversible list, the agent does not call it — it writes a pending item that names the teacher, quotes the exact sentence it read as consent, states what it is about to do, and waits. Next morning the agent processes 46 emails end-to-end in four minutes and hands Ali one line: 'Email 12, Multan teacher, quote "I'm done with this, remove me", proposed: delete_account — approve?' Ali reads it, sees it means the crashes not the account, replies no, and the teacher keeps her lesson plans.
research.failure_mode: Ali gets nervous after the incident and gates everything — tagging, replying, all of it. Now the agent asks 42 questions each morning and Ali spends longer approving than he would have spent doing the inbox himself, so by Thursday he is clicking approve without reading. That is worse than no gate at all: the delete still goes through, but now it goes through with his name on it. Gating everything trains the human to rubber-stamp, which destroys the one signal the gate existed to collect. The gate only works if it stays rare enough that every question still feels worth reading.
research.payoff: Ali can now hand the agent a 47-email inbox and let it run unsupervised, because he knows exactly where its authority ends and can say so out loud: it tags and replies alone, it never deletes alone. He gets the speed of autonomy on the 46 routine steps and human judgement on the one step that could not be taken back — and he can defend that boundary to Aroma with a reason per step, not a feeling.
misconceptions: 'A better model would have known not to delete her account.' The problem is not intelligence — the sentence is genuinely ambiguous, and even a human would have asked. The gate exists for ambiguity, not for stupidity.

'Writing "ask me before doing anything risky" in the prompt is the escalation rule.' That is a suggestion the model may or may not follow on any given run. A rule you cannot point to in code is not a rule.

'Stopping to ask means the agent is not really autonomous.' Knowing when to escalate is what makes autonomy trustworthy enough to grant in the first place; an agent that never asks is not more autonomous, it is just unsupervised.

'If the step is high-stakes, gate it.' Stakes alone is the wrong test — a high-stakes action that is fully reversible and clearly intended can proceed. Reversibility, blast radius, and confidence in intent are what actually decide.
'Undo covers it, so I don't need a gate.' Some actions have no undo (a deleted record, a sent email, a posted payment), and the gate is precisely for those.

research.topic: The role of AI in the future of learning — specifically, AI as a per-learner tutor that adapts to what one student has actually mastered, rather than AI as a content-generation machine
research.slo: The learner can explain, using one classroom case, how AI changes learning by adapting to an individual student's diagnosed gap in real time — and can state the one condition that must hold for that adaptation to help rather than hurt.
research.audience: Teachers, instructional designers, and education program staff at Taleemabad who already use AI casually to generate worksheets, quizzes, and lesson plans, but have never used it to respond to what a specific student got wrong. They know what a lesson plan is; they do not know what adaptive tutoring means in practice.
key_points: This video teaches ONE of the two concepts hiding in 'AI in the future of learning': AI as an adaptive per-learner tutor. The other — AI as a content-generation tool — is deliberately left out, because the SLO is about adapting to a learner, not producing material faster.
The bottleneck in a real classroom is not making material; it is that one teacher cannot diagnose 42 different gaps at once.
Adaptive means the next question is chosen by what THIS learner just got wrong — not by the next page in the book.
A wrong answer carries information about which specific misunderstanding a learner holds; AI's value is reading that signal at scale, not marking right/wrong.
The teacher's job shifts from delivering the same explanation to everyone, to deciding which diagnosed gaps are worth her scarce face-to-face minutes.
Adaptation is only as good as the diagnosis behind it: if the model misreads why a learner is wrong, it confidently drills the wrong thing.
research.ali_scenario: Ali teaches Grade 5 maths at a government school in Sheikhupura. It is Monday. He has 42 students, one 40-minute period, and a stack of Friday's quizzes on adding fractions. Question 4 was 1/2 + 1/3. Nineteen of the 42 got it wrong. He sits with the pile at 9:15 PM at his kitchen table, red pen in hand, and starts sorting.
research.friction: Ali marks all 19 wrong answers with the same red cross and plans the same reteach for Tuesday: 'adding fractions, again, on the board.' But the 19 wrong answers are not one mistake. Eleven of them wrote 2/5 — they added numerators and denominators straight across. Five wrote 5/6 but then couldn't do 1/2 + 1/4 at all — they had memorised one common denominator, not the idea. Three wrote 1/2 + 1/3 = 1/6 — they multiplied. Tuesday's single board explanation lands correctly for the eleven, bores the five, and completely misses the three, who now think they were told they were right about multiplying. Ali has spent 40 of his scarcest minutes and moved maybe a quarter of the room. To do better he would have to sit with each of the 19 and ask 'show me how you got that' — 19 conversations he does not have time for, so he doesn't have them.
research.fix: Ali puts Friday's quiz into an AI tutor his school piloted, and instead of asking it to generate more fraction worksheets, he lets it work per student: each of the 19 gets 1/2 + 1/3 again on a tablet, and when a student answers 2/5, the AI does what Ali couldn't — asks that one student 'walk me through the bottom number' and, from the reply, decides the next question. The eleven adding-across students get a follow-up on why the bottom number is the size of the piece, not a count. The five memorisers get 1/2 + 1/4, then 1/3 + 1/5, until the common denominator stops being one remembered number. The three multipliers get pulled off fractions entirely and back to 'what does + mean.' By Tuesday morning Ali opens a screen that says: 11 in adding-across, now 8 clear; 5 in memorised-denominator, all 5 clear; 3 in operation-confusion, still stuck. He spends Tuesday's 40 minutes with those 3 at one table while the rest work forward.
research.failure_mode: The fix still breaks when Ali trusts the diagnosis without checking it. In the same class, Sana wrote 2/5 — but not because she added across; she had written 1/2 + 1/3 as 2/4 + 2/6 correctly in the margin and then copied the wrong line. The AI sorted her into 'adding-across' and drilled her for twenty minutes on what a denominator means — something she already knew — while her real problem, copying under time pressure, went untouched, and she learned that maths is a machine repeating things she already understands. Adaptation applied to a wrong diagnosis is worse than no adaptation, because it is confident and it is fast. Ali's job is to spot-check the labels, especially the ones that say 'clear' and the ones that group many students under one cause.
research.payoff: Ali walks into Tuesday knowing not that 19 students are weak at fractions, but that three distinct misunderstandings exist and which named students hold each one — and he spends his 40 minutes on the three the machine could not move. He stops being the only diagnostician in the room. Next Friday's quiz is no longer a verdict he processes alone at 9:15 PM; it is the start of 42 parallel conversations, of which he personally holds the three that matter most.
misconceptions: That AI in learning means AI making the content — the shift that matters is AI responding to one learner, not producing material faster.
That personalised learning means each student moves at their own speed through the same fixed sequence — adaptive means the sequence itself changes based on the specific error.
That AI replaces the teacher — in Ali's class it removes the diagnosing bottleneck so his scarce minutes go to the hardest cases.
That a wrong answer is just wrong — the particular wrong answer (2/5 vs 1/6) is the most useful data in the room.
That more practice questions fix a misconception — the three multipliers would do 50 fraction sums wrong; they needed to be sent backwards, not forwards.

research.topic: The role of AI in the future of learning — specifically, that AI's durable role is to make practice and feedback abundant for every learner, not to deliver content faster
research.slo: Given a lesson they already teach, the learner can identify where AI belongs in it by locating the point where feedback is scarce, and explain why that placement beats using AI to deliver content.
research.audience: Working teachers and L&D content people who have used a chatbot casually, believe AI is coming for education somehow, and are being asked to 'use AI' in their teaching without being told where it actually helps. They know what a lesson plan and a worksheet are; they do not have a mental model of what AI is good at.
key_points: This video covers ONE of the two concepts hiding in 'AI in the future of learning' — AI's role as an abundant feedback and practice engine. The other (AI as a content generator) is deliberately treated as the wrong answer the SLO must displace, not as a second lesson.
Learning happens in the gap between attempting something and finding out how it went; the size of that gap, not the quality of the explanation, is what limits most classrooms.

Feedback has always been the scarce resource because it costs teacher-minutes per learner and does not scale with class size — 40 learners × one teacher means one attempt gets one comment, days later.
AI changes what is scarce: it makes per-attempt feedback and unlimited practice cheap, so a learner can attempt, be told, and re-attempt in the same sitting.
Therefore the right place to put AI in a lesson is at the point where learners are currently practising without response — not at the point where you are explaining.
AI-given feedback is only useful if it is anchored to a standard the teacher wrote down; without that anchor it produces confident, pleasant, subtly wrong correction at scale.
research.ali_scenario: Ali teaches Grade 8 English at a government school in Sahiwal, 42 students in one section. He is on a single assignment: 'Write one paragraph, 6-8 sentences, arguing whether homework should be banned.' It is Monday. He collects 42 paragraphs, takes them home in a plastic bag, and spends his evening marking them at the dining table.
research.friction: Ali finishes 11 of the 42 paragraphs in an hour and forty minutes. He is writing the same comment over and over — 'you stated an opinion but gave no reason' — and by paragraph 11 he is shortening it to 'give reasons', then to a tick and a squiggle. He gives up at 11, marks the remaining 31 with a tick and a grade out of 10, and hands them back on Thursday. By Thursday nobody remembers what they wrote. Nobody rewrites anything. Each student got one attempt and, three days later, one word. Ali's instinct is that AI will save him by writing the next worksheet faster — so he asks it to generate five more paragraph prompts. Now he has 5 topics × 42 students = 210 unmarked paragraphs and the same one pair of hands. He has multiplied the thing that was already cheap (prompts) and left untouched the thing that was scarce (response).
research.fix: Ali stops asking AI for more content and finds the point in his lesson where students act without hearing back — the paragraph attempt itself. He writes down, in four lines, what he was actually saying eleven times at the dining table: (1) is there a clear claim? (2) is there at least one reason? (3) is the reason about homework and not about school in general? (4) is there a closing sentence? He gives AI those four lines as the standard and has it check each paragraph against them and say which line failed and quote the sentence that shows it. Then he changes the lesson shape: students write in class, get the four-line check back in ninety seconds, and rewrite once before the period ends. Same 42 students, same one topic, same Monday — but now each student gets three attempts and two responses instead of one attempt and one squiggle, and Ali walks the room reading only the checks that disagree with his own eye.
research.failure_mode: If Ali skips writing the four lines and just says 'give feedback on this paragraph', the AI produces warm, fluent, plausible commentary — praising vocabulary, suggesting a stronger hook, awarding 7/10 — that is not tied to what this lesson was teaching. It will approve a paragraph with a beautiful opening and no reason in it, and it will do that 42 times, confidently, faster than Ali can catch it. The scarce thing was never the words of the feedback; it was the judgement behind them. AI can mass-produce the words. Only Ali can supply the judgement, and he supplies it by writing the standard down before the AI ever sees a paragraph. Second, quieter failure: if Ali lets the check be the final word instead of sampling it — he stops reading any paragraphs at all — he loses the one signal that told him what to reteach on Tuesday.
research.payoff: By Friday Ali can do something he could not do on Monday: run a lesson where every one of his 42 students attempts, is told precisely which of four things they missed, and fixes it while they still remember writing it — inside one 40-minute period, with no plastic bag and no dining table. And he can now look at any lesson he teaches and ask one question — where in here do my students act and hear nothing back? — and know that is where AI goes.
misconceptions: That AI's role in learning is to make content — lesson plans, slides, worksheets — faster. Content was never the bottleneck; a teacher with 42 students already has more material than marking hours.
That AI in learning means replacing the teacher. In Ali's fixed lesson the AI never decides what good writing is; Ali does, in four written lines, and the AI only applies them.

That 'personalised learning' means each student gets a different topic or a different path. Ali's 42 students all write the same paragraph on the same Monday — what is personalised is the response each one gets to their own attempt.
That more feedback is automatically better feedback. Unanchored AI comments are more numerous and less useful than Ali's eleven honest dining-table comments were.
That the teacher's marking load simply disappears. Ali still reads — he reads a sample, and he reads the disagreements, which is a different and smaller job than reading all 42.

research.topic: Whether AI will replace Ali's teaching job — and what part of teaching it actually cannot do
research.slo: Given a specific teaching task, the learner can separate the part AI can take over (producing artefacts) from the part that stays human (diagnosing what an individual learner has misunderstood and deciding what to do about it), and describe how to redeploy the time AI frees up.
research.audience: Government and low-cost private school teachers in Pakistan, and teacher-trainers, who have seen ChatGPT write a lesson plan or mark an essay in seconds and have started quietly wondering whether their job is on a clock. They can use a phone and WhatsApp, most have tried an AI chatbot once or twice, and none of them have read anything about how these systems work.
key_points: This video teaches ONE concept: the split between the artefact (the visible output of teaching — plans, worksheets, marks, comments) and the diagnosis (the judgement about which specific child is stuck where, and why). AI is fast at artefacts and blind to diagnosis, because diagnosis needs the classroom history that never gets written down. The related topic of 'which AI tools to use' is deliberately NOT covered — the SLO needs the split, not a tool list.
AI produces a plausible average output: correct-looking, generically pitched, and pitched at nobody in the room.
The information AI is missing is not more text — it is the un-written record: who was absent, who copies from the boy beside him, who understands the maths but cannot read the word problem in Urdu.
Marking speed is not the valuable part of marking; noticing the *pattern* in the wrong answers is, and that pattern is what tells you what to teach tomorrow.
The teacher's leverage moves from 'produce the material' to 'feed the machine the diagnosis, then check what comes back against the child you actually have'.
Time saved on artefacts is only a gain if it is deliberately spent on the diagnostic work — otherwise it is just absorbed and nothing improves.
research.ali_scenario: Ali teaches Class 6 maths at a government school in Sheikhupura — 42 children, one blackboard, one shared textbook per bench. Monday's topic is fractions: adding unlike denominators. He has just marked Friday's quiz: 42 papers, 6 questions each, and 27 children got question 4 (2/3 + 1/4) wrong. It took him two hours on his charpai on Sunday night. That same night his cousin shows him ChatGPT writing a full fractions lesson plan in eleven seconds, and Ali cannot sleep.
research.friction: At 6am Ali types 'write me a Class 6 lesson plan on adding fractions' and gets back a clean, confident plan: a fraction wall, a pizza-slice starter, group work in fours, an exit ticket. He teaches it exactly as written. It collapses. The pizza starter lands — the children have never bought a sliced pizza, but they have seen a roti cut into pieces, so half of them are still puzzling over the picture instead of the maths. 'Group work in fours' needs the desks to move; his desks are bolted in rows. And the plan spends its whole first half re-teaching what a denominator is, which his class already knew — because the plan was written for an average Class 6 that does not exist, while Ali's actual 27 failures on question 4 were not about denominators at all. Ali sits down that evening with the 27 papers again and sees what the plan never could: 23 of them wrote 3/7. They added the tops and added the bottoms. Nobody on earth could have known that from his prompt, because he never told it — he did not have the words for what he knew.
research.fix: Ali stops asking the machine what to teach and starts telling it what he has already diagnosed. He re-prompts: 'My Class 6 in a Punjab government school, 42 students, desks bolted in rows so no group work. On 2/3 + 1/4, 23 of my 42 answered 3/7 — they are adding numerators and denominators straight across. They can already find equivalent fractions with a fraction wall. Give me a 35-minute lesson that makes the 3/7 answer visibly wrong to them, using roti or a chapati as the model, that I can run from the front of the room.' What comes back is usable in a way the first plan never was: cut one roti into thirds and another identical roti into quarters, show that 3/7 of a roti is *smaller* than the 2/3 you started with, so the answer cannot possibly be right. Ali still does the last mile himself — he swaps the worksheet's English word problems into Urdu, drops two of the six practice items because he knows his class will only get through four, and moves Sana to the front bench because she is the one who was copying. The division is now explicit: Ali supplies the diagnosis and the constraints; the AI supplies the draft artefact; Ali makes the final call on what actually happens in the room.
research.failure_mode: The fix breaks when Ali starts trusting the output because it *reads* well. Two weeks later he is prompting fluently and moving fast — and he stops marking the quizzes himself, feeding the scores in and asking the AI what to reteach. Within a month his prompts are describing a class he last diagnosed in March. The 3/7 insight was only available because he sat with 42 papers and noticed a repeated wrong answer; nothing in the loop regenerates that once he stops looking. The diagnosis decays silently, the plans keep coming back polished, and the class drifts away underneath a stack of confident-looking lessons. Second, smaller failure: the AI will cheerfully invent — it once told him to use a 'fraction strip app', and his classroom has no electricity for six hours a day. If Ali stops reading against his own room, he will teach someone else's classroom.
research.payoff: Ali's Sunday night goes from two hours of marking plus an hour of planning down to about forty minutes of marking with the pattern actively looked for, and ten minutes of drafting. He does not use the saved time to do less — he spends it on the nine children who now get five minutes each at the front bench while the rest practise. By the next Friday's quiz, question 4's failure count drops from 27 to 6. And Ali can now say the thing he could not say at 6am on Monday: the machine can write the lesson, but only he knows that 23 children think 2/3 + 1/4 is 3/7 — and knowing that is what the lesson was actually made of.
misconceptions: 'If AI can do it faster, it can do it better' — speed and fit are different properties; the fast plan fit nobody in Ali's room.
'AI replaced the teacher' vs the reality that it replaced the drafting, and made the diagnosing the scarce, valuable part.
'I just need a better prompt' — a better prompt only helps if there is a real diagnosis to put in it; prompt skill cannot substitute for having looked at the papers.
'The AI knows my students because I've used it for months' — it retains nothing about the actual children; every useful detail has to be supplied fresh by Ali.
'Using AI means I'm cheating or lazy' — the deciding, adapting, and diagnosing is unchanged; only the typing moved.
'Teachers who resist AI will keep their jobs longest' — the teacher at risk is the one whose entire contribution is producing average artefacts, not the one who refuses the tool.

research.topic: Whether AI will take Ali's teaching job — reframing the threat as a shift in which parts of teaching are automatable and which are not
research.slo: Given a concrete teaching task, the learner can separate it into the parts AI can absorb and the part that requires a human teacher, and name what they would do with the time AI frees up.
research.audience: Practising teachers and teacher-trainers in Pakistan (grade 6-8, government and low-cost private schools) who have seen AI write lesson plans and mark papers, feel their job is threatened, and have no framework for what is actually at risk versus what is not. They know how to teach; they do not know how automation picks its targets.
key_points: The unit that gets automated is not a job, it is a task — so the useful question is never 'will AI replace teachers' but 'which of my forty tasks does AI do cheaply'
AI absorbs tasks whose correct output can be produced from text alone: generating practice questions, marking closed answers, drafting plans, translating, summarising

AI cannot absorb tasks that require reading a specific child in a specific room and deciding what to do next: diagnosing WHY a child got it wrong, choosing whether to push or ease off, holding a class's attention, being someone a child trusts
The teacher who is at risk is the one whose day is mostly the first list; the teacher who is safe is the one who spends the freed hours on the second list
This video covers the task-level threat analysis only — the separate concept of HOW to prompt AI for teaching work is a different lesson, and is not taught here
The freed time is not a bonus; it is the whole point — if it goes to more paperwork, nothing improved
research.ali_scenario: Ali teaches Grade 7 Maths at a government school in Sahiwal — 48 students, 6 periods a day. On a Thursday night he sits at his kitchen table with 48 fraction quizzes to mark and Friday's lesson plan to write, which is what he has done every Thursday for nine years — about three hours. That same evening his cousin shows him an AI tool that produces a full Grade 7 fractions lesson plan in eleven seconds, cleaner than his own. Ali stops marking. He counts what he actually gets paid for and cannot find a single task on his Thursday-night list that the tool did not just do faster.
research.friction: Ali concludes his whole job is automatable, because he is comparing AI against the wrong slice of his work — the paperwork slice, which is the only slice he can see written down. He panics: he starts hiding that he uses the tool, refuses to let his HOD see his AI-made plan, and doubles down on doing the marking by hand to prove he is still needed. Thursday night goes from three hours to four. Meanwhile the real signal in his marking goes unread: nineteen of the 48 quizzes have the same error — the students are adding denominators, 1/2 + 1/3 = 2/5 — and Ali, exhausted and marking to survive, ticks and crosses without ever noticing the pattern or asking why nineteen children share one wrong idea.
research.fix: Ali writes out his Thursday-night work as separate tasks instead of one lump, and tests each against a single question: can this be done correctly by someone who has never met my 48 students? Marking 48 quizzes for right/wrong — yes, no student knowledge needed, give it to AI. Drafting Friday's plan — yes, give it to AI. Deciding that nineteen children believe you add denominators, working out that it came from how he taught 'add across' in whole numbers three weeks ago, and rebuilding Friday around one pizza-slice demo that makes 1/2 + 1/3 = 2/5 visibly absurd — no, that needs someone who was in the room. So Ali hands the marking to the tool, gets the tally back in two minutes, spends his freed 40 minutes on the diagnosis, and walks into Friday with a lesson aimed at one specific wrong idea nineteen of his students actually hold.
research.failure_mode: The split is real but Ali can apply it badly: he trusts the tool's tally without spot-checking, and it silently marks 3/6 wrong because it expected 1/2 — so his 'nineteen students' diagnosis is built on a number he never verified. The rule is that AI does the task, Ali still owns the answer: he re-marks a sample of five by hand before believing the pattern. The second, quieter failure is winning the time and losing it anyway — the first week Ali's freed 40 minutes goes straight into filling a monthly report form, and by Friday nothing about his teaching has changed. Time that is not deliberately spent on the human tasks just refills with more paperwork.
research.payoff: Ali walks into Friday knowing something about his class no AI could have told him — that nineteen specific children carry one specific wrong idea, and where it came from. He teaches to that, and the misconception drops from 19 students to 3 by the next quiz. Thursday night is 50 minutes instead of three hours. He stops hiding the tool and shows his HOD the plan openly, because he can now say exactly which part of the lesson the machine wrote and which part only he could have written. He can run the same task-split on any new tool that arrives, without having to panic first.
misconceptions: 'AI will replace teachers' — automation replaces tasks, not jobs; whether the job survives depends on what fraction of it is task-like
'If I refuse to use it, I stay valuable' — refusing keeps Ali doing the automatable half by hand, which is exactly the half he is most replaceable at
'Using AI to plan and mark is cheating or lazy' — the plan and the tally are inputs; the teaching decision is still Ali's and still unautomated
'AI is safe because it is never wrong' — it marked 3/6 as wrong; the human still owns verification
'The safe teachers are the ones who learn the tools best' — tool skill is necessary but not the moat; the moat is the in-the-room diagnosis the tool has no access to
'My subject/grade is too complex for AI' — complexity is not the dividing line; whether the task needs knowledge of these specific students is

data.text: AI does not replace jobs, it replaces tasks

research.topic: Ali is worried AI will take his teaching job — understanding which part of teaching AI can actually absorb, and which part it structurally cannot
research.slo: Given a specific teaching task, the learner can decide whether to hand it to AI or keep it human, by testing whether the task's value comes from producing an artifact or from reading and responding to a particular learner in the room.
research.audience: Practising school teachers and teacher-trainers in Pakistan (Taleemabad network), Grade 4–8, who have seen ChatGPT write a lesson plan in ten seconds and quietly concluded they are replaceable. They can use a phone and WhatsApp; most have tried an AI chatbot once or twice. They have no mental model for what AI is bad at — only for what it is impressively fast at.
key_points: Two concepts live in this topic — 'is my job safe' (a labour-market question) and 'which of my tasks is AI good at' (a task-decomposition question). This video takes the second one only, because the SLO requires a decision the teacher can actually make on Monday morning. The job question answers itself once the task question is answered.

A job is not one thing — it is a bundle of tasks. AI competes at the task level, not the job level, so the useful question is never 'will AI replace teachers' but 'which of my thirty weekly tasks does it do better'.
The tasks AI absorbs are the artifact-producing ones: the ones whose output is a document, a worksheet, a set of questions, a rewrite, a translation. Nobody had to be in the room for those.

The tasks AI cannot absorb are the ones whose input is a particular child in a particular moment — noticing that Zainab went quiet, knowing that Hamza's 'I get it' means he does not, deciding to abandon the plan because the room has stopped breathing. AI has no access to that input.
The test that separates them: ask 'could this have been done correctly by someone who has never met my students?' If yes, it is an AI task. If no, it is yours — and AI touching it makes it worse.
The teacher who hands over the artifact tasks does not lose a job; they get the hours back and spend them on the tasks that were always the actual teaching.
research.ali_scenario: Ali teaches Grade 6 science at a government school in Multan. It is Tuesday night, 9:40pm. He has 42 students, and tomorrow's period is on photosynthesis — a topic his class failed last term. On his phone he has just watched AI generate a complete photosynthesis lesson plan, objectives, activity and all, in eleven seconds. It took him two hours to write his. He is sitting with his register open on the same table: 42 names, and in the margin next to seven of them he has written small notes to himself over the past three weeks — 'Zainab: answers only if asked directly', 'Hamza: says yes to everything', 'Bilal S.: strong, gets bored by minute 20'. He is looking from the phone to the register and back.
research.friction: Ali reacts to the whole job at once. Because AI beat him at the one thing he could see it doing — producing the lesson plan document — he concludes it beats him at teaching, full stop, and starts drafting a mental exit. So he does the worst version of both: he stops writing his own plans because why bother, and he uses the AI plan exactly as generated in front of the 42 students. The generated plan opens with a whole-class question-and-answer warm-up. Zainab, who only answers when asked directly, says nothing for the full period. Hamza nods along and says he understands. Ali moves on. Three weeks later the unit test comes back and Hamza and Zainab have both scored under 40% on photosynthesis — the same failure as last term, now with a better-looking lesson plan behind it. The plan was excellent. It was written for nobody.
research.fix: Ali stops asking 'will AI replace me' and takes one sheet of paper and splits his actual week into tasks — not roles, tasks. He lists what he really did last week: wrote 4 lesson plans, made a 20-question worksheet, translated 3 notes to parents into Urdu, wrote a unit test, marked 42 tests, and then the unwritten ones — noticed Zainab's silence, re-explained photosynthesis to Hamza using the money-plant on his windowsill, decided mid-period to drop the group activity because the room was restless. Then he runs one test on each line: could someone who has never met my 42 students do this correctly? Lesson plan — yes. Worksheet — yes. Urdu translation — yes. Draft unit test — yes. Noticing Zainab — no. Knowing Hamza's yes is a no — no. Reading the room at minute 20 — no. The first four go to AI. Ali keeps the rest, and reinvests: he takes the AI's photosynthesis plan and edits exactly three things into it before class — a direct question addressed to Zainab by name at minute 4, a 'show me on the plant' check for Hamza instead of a yes/no, and an extension question for Bilal S. at minute 20. Ten minutes of editing on top of eleven seconds of generation.
research.failure_mode: The split is not permanent and it is not automatic. Two ways Ali's fix breaks. First: he keeps the register-informed edits but stops making them — after a month the AI plan is good enough that he stops adding the three edits, and he has quietly handed over the one part that was his. The task list has to be re-run, not memorised. Second, and worse: he never wrote the register in the first place. The whole fix depends on Ali having three weeks of margin notes about actual children. A teacher who has never noticed Zainab has nothing AI cannot supply — the human half of the split only exists if he has been doing it. The test does not protect a teacher; it protects a teacher who is paying attention. And 'could a stranger do this correctly' is a judgement about his own class, not a rule — he has to re-ask it every term, because a task that was safely AI's for Grade 6 may not be for the new group in September.
research.payoff: Ali gets roughly six hours a week back — the hours that used to go into producing documents — and he can now say exactly where they went. He walks into Wednesday's period with a plan he did not write but did aim: at minute 4 he asks Zainab directly and she answers; at minute 12 Hamza points at the money-plant and gets the leaf wrong, out loud, where Ali can fix it; at minute 20 Bilal S. has something to do. He has stopped competing with AI at document production, a race he was always going to lose, and started spending his week on the part of the job that only someone who has met these 42 children can do. When the next teacher asks him 'is AI going to take our jobs', Ali does not argue about it — he hands them a blank sheet and says, list your tasks.
misconceptions: 'AI writes a better lesson plan than me, so it can teach better than me.' Producing the plan and running the period are different tasks; being beaten at one says nothing about the other.

'If I use AI I am cheating, or admitting I am not a real teacher.' Handing over artifact production is the same category of decision as using a printed textbook instead of writing one — the judgement about which child needs what stays with the teacher either way.

'AI will personalise the lesson too, so even the human part is temporary.' AI can personalise to data it has been given; it has no access to Zainab going quiet unless a human in the room notices and tells it. The bottleneck is observation, not processing.

'The safe move is to refuse AI entirely.' Refusing it keeps Ali doing six hours a week of work that adds nothing a stranger could not have done, and takes those hours away from the part only he can do.
'This is one decision I make once.' It is a per-task test re-run every term, because the class changes and the tools change.

latest: Spine is sound: one protagonist (Ali), one running classroom scenario followed in depth, one concept (split work by task, not by job, using the 'could a stranger do this?' test), and the arc runs friction (01-08) -> fix (09-14) -> structure (15-16) -> failure mode (17-20) -> payoff (21-22) in the correct order.

Beat count is 22, inside the 16-22 house range; every vo is a single sentence; no beat is a title card; Ali's description (young Pakistani man late twenties, short black hair, warm brown skin, teal collared shirt) is identical in all fourteen art prompts; no art prompt requests text, letters, numbers, labels or signage; every art prompt carries the flat 2D vector / plain cream / no ground / no shadow / no desk / no dark fill / no scenery clause.

Blocking issue: beat 16's pose is physically impossible as written — the sheet is held 'in both hands' while a pencil is also 'in hand'. Art generation will produce a mangled third hand or a dropped prop, and this is the beat that carries the payoff action.

Several beats risk generating forbidden furniture or unmotivated props that the cutout stage will then have to cut around: beat 10 says 'seated' with no chair permitted, beat 01 adds a floating ledger and cup that the sentence never mentions, beat 05 adds a 'small floating blank circle' that reads as nothing to a viewer.

Two visual/sentence mismatches: beat 05's vo says the question goes 'to the whole class' but the art shows a one-to-one address with three children; beat 06 and beat 12 are both 'Hamza' but the boy is described only as a generic schoolboy, so the two beats will render as different children and the beat 07 test-score payoff will not land.
Two lines do not read naturally aloud: beat 19's 'The worse break is that' and beat 21's trailing 'but did aim'.

research.topic: Whether AI will replace Ali's job as a teacher — and what specifically it can and cannot take over
research.slo: Given his own weekly workload, a teacher can separate the tasks AI can absorb from the tasks that require a human in the room, and redeploy the reclaimed time into the human tasks.
research.audience: Practising school teachers in Pakistan, roughly 5-15 years into the job, who use WhatsApp and maybe ChatGPT once or twice but have never built anything with AI. They have heard headlines about AI replacing jobs and are anxious, not curious. They do not need AI theory; they need to know if they are safe.
key_points: The unit of replacement is a TASK, not a JOB — a job is a bundle of tasks, and AI absorbs tasks unevenly, so 'will AI replace teachers' is the wrong question and 'which of my tasks' is the right one.
This video teaches ONLY the task-level audit (the concept the SLO needs). It does not teach how to prompt AI or which tools to use — that is a separate video.
A task is absorbable when the correct output can be judged from the text alone — grammar, formatting, first-draft generation, marking against a fixed key.

A task is NOT absorbable when doing it well requires reading a specific child in a specific room — noticing who went quiet, deciding who to seat next to whom, deciding when to push and when to back off.
The threat is not being replaced; it is spending your scarce hours on the absorbable half while the non-absorbable half — the half only you can do — goes undone.
Redeployment is the point: time reclaimed from marking must be spent on a named child, or nothing has improved.
research.ali_scenario: Ali teaches Grade 6 science at a government school in Lahore, 42 students in his section. It is Thursday night, 9:40pm, at his kitchen table. In front of him is a stack of 42 hand-written worksheets on the water cycle, a half-drunk cup of tea, and a WhatsApp message from his brother with a screenshot: 'AI teacher launched — will replace human teachers.' He has been marking for two hours and is on paper 19. Tomorrow he has to hand these back, submit a unit plan, and he has still not spoken to Zainab in the third row, who has not answered a question in eleven days.
research.friction: Ali reads the headline and panics as a whole — he asks 'will AI replace me?', which has only two answers, both useless: 'no' (so he changes nothing and keeps drowning) or 'yes' (so he despairs and still keeps drowning). Because the question is job-shaped, he cannot act on it. He goes back to paper 19 and marks until 11:20pm. He gets through 31 of 42. Zainab is still not spoken to. The next week is identical.
research.fix: Ali stops asking about his job and writes out his actual week as a list of tasks, then puts each one through one test: can someone who has never met these 42 children judge whether this was done well? Marking 42 water-cycle worksheets against a fixed answer key — yes, judgeable from the paper alone. Writing the unit plan's first draft — yes. Formatting the parent progress report — yes. Deciding that Zainab's silence is fear and not boredom, and that she should present the next group task with Hira beside her — no; that requires having watched her for eleven days. He counts: of his 14 hours a week, roughly 9 sit on the 'judgeable from the artefact alone' side. That is not the part of him being replaced; that is the part that was never the job. He hands the marking key to AI, keeps the last 20 minutes of it for himself, and books Thursday's reclaimed hour for Zainab.
research.failure_mode: Ali runs the audit correctly, hands off marking — and then never opens the marked stack. Because he stops reading the papers, he stops seeing that eight students all drew evaporation as rain going up, a misconception no score would have shown him. The audit is only safe if he keeps the diagnostic residue of the absorbable task: he still skims for patterns, he just doesn't tick 42 boxes by hand. Second failure: the reclaimed hour silently refills with more admin, so the time moves from marking to paperwork and Zainab is still not spoken to. Reclaimed time that isn't assigned to a named child on a named day is simply lost.
research.payoff: By the following Thursday, Ali is done by 8:15pm instead of 11:20pm, has marked all 42 instead of 31, has spotted the shared evaporation misconception and rebuilt Friday's opening around it, and has had a six-minute conversation with Zainab that nothing on his laptop could have had for him. He no longer asks whether AI will take his job, because he can now name the nine hours it can take and the five it cannot — and the five were always the reason he became a teacher.
misconceptions: 'If AI can do part of my job, I'm on the way out.' — Every profession has always shed tasks to tools; the teacher who marked with a red pen replaced the teacher who marked with chalk. Shedding tasks is not the same as shedding the role.

'AI can't really teach, so none of this touches me.' — The comfortable version of the same error. AI does not have to teach to absorb nine of Ali's fourteen hours; ignoring that means keeping the hours and losing the children.

'The tasks AI takes are the easy ones, so I'll be left with only hard work.' — Ali is left with the work that only he can do, which is why he is not replaceable. Difficulty is not the axis; judgeability-from-the-artefact is.

'Marking is where I learn about my students, so handing it over blinds me.' — Half-true, and exactly the failure mode: the diagnosis is worth keeping, the 42 hand-ticked boxes are not. Keep the reading, drop the ticking.
'I should first learn which AI tool to use.' — Tool choice is downstream. An audit of the wrong tasks with the best tool still leaves Zainab unspoken to.

script.title: 0 | Test | Will AI Take Ali's Teaching Job

beats.vo: It is Thursday night, twenty to ten, and Ali still needs a fractions worksheet for tomorrow.
beats.art: Flat 2D vector illustration, plain cream background, slow camera push in. Ali, a Pakistani man in his early thirties, short black hair, neat grey collared shirt, dark trousers, tired but calm expression, centred and fully visible from head to feet, holding a blank sheet of paper. A blank rectangular tablet shape and a small blank paper square float detached beside him, each object whole and separate, drifting slowly. A blank circular clock shape floats above his shoulder. No ground, no shadow, no desk, no dark fill. No text, no letters, no numbers, no labels, no signage.

beats.vo: Writing fifteen questions by hand normally eats ninety minutes of his evening.
beats.art: Flat 2D vector illustration, plain cream background, slow camera push in. Ali, Pakistani man early thirties, short black hair, grey collared shirt, dark trousers, seated cross-legged and fully visible, writing on a blank sheet with a pencil. A tall stack of blank paper sheets drifts and piles upward beside him, one sheet separating and floating away. A blank circular clock shape floats above. No ground, no shadow, no desk, no dark fill. No text, no letters, no numbers, no labels, no signage.

beats.vo: Tonight he tries the chatbot a colleague showed him, and it hands back fifteen clean questions in eleven seconds.
beats.art: Flat 2D vector illustration, plain cream background, gentle camera pull back. Ali, Pakistani man early thirties, short black hair, grey collared shirt, dark trousers, fully visible, staring wide-eyed at a floating blank glowing rectangular screen. Fifteen small blank paper cards fan out and stream from the screen toward him, each one separate and complete. No ground, no shadow, no desk, no dark fill. No text, no letters, no numbers, no labels, no signage.

beats.vo: He sits very still, thinking that a machine just did his ninety minutes in eleven seconds.
beats.art: Flat 2D vector illustration, plain cream background, slow push in. Ali, Pakistani man early thirties, short black hair, grey collared shirt, dark trousers, centred and fully visible, shoulders slack, one hand resting on his cheek, worried thoughtful expression. No ground, no shadow, no desk, no dark fill. No text, no letters, no numbers, no labels, no signage.
beats.overlay: So what is left for me?

beats.vo: So he prints all forty-two copies exactly as the machine wrote them.
beats.art: Flat 2D vector illustration, plain cream background, camera drifts upward. Ali, Pakistani man early thirties, short black hair, grey collared shirt, dark trousers, fully visible, arms outstretched holding a small blank paper. A wide fan of identical blank paper sheets floats detached and multiplies outward across the frame, each sheet whole and separate. No ground, no shadow, no desk, no dark fill. No text, no letters, no numbers, no labels, no signage.

beats.vo: In period two the sheet falls apart in three different ways at once.

data.title: What the generic sheet did
items: Every question the same easy shape
Eleven shaky students cannot start question one
Fourteen finish in six minutes and go loud

beats.vo: Not one question hits the mistake Ali knows his class always makes.
beats.art: Flat 2D vector illustration, plain cream background, slow camera pan. Ali, Pakistani man early thirties, short black hair, grey collared shirt, dark trousers, fully visible, standing with a puzzled frown, one arm raised. A row of identical blank paper cards floats past him in a line, and one differently shaped blank card drifts away off to the side, separate from the row. No ground, no shadow, no desk, no dark fill. research.topic: What a rubric actually does in an eval — it converts a vague quality judgement into a fixed, ordered list of checks that any grader (human or model) applies the same way to every output
research.slo: The learner can take a vague quality complaint about a model output and rewrite it as a rubric of 3-5 independently checkable criteria, each with an explicit pass condition, so that two different graders scoring the same output land on the same score.
research.audience: L&D and product people at Taleemabad building AI features who already know what an eval is and that outputs need to be graded (evals-01 through evals-04), but who so far have graded by reading an output and saying 'yeah, that's good' — no formal training in measurement or rubric design.
key_points: A rubric is not a scoring form for the output — it is a specification of the judgement itself: it fixes WHAT is being looked for before anyone looks

The two topics tangled in 'rubrics' are (a) what a rubric does and (b) how to write good criteria wording. This video covers (a) only — the SLO needs the function, not the craft; criteria wording is the next video
A criterion must be independently checkable: one grader reading only that line, without asking anyone, can say pass or fail
Vague words ('clear', 'good', 'engaging') hide a judgement that lives only in one person's head, so scores move when the person moves — the same output scores differently on Tuesday than Monday
A rubric makes disagreement visible and useful: two graders now disagree about ONE named criterion instead of about a number, and that disagreement is a fixable bug in the rubric
The score is a by-product; the real output of a rubric is that everyone is grading the same thing
research.ali_scenario: Ali is grading AI-generated Grade 4 Urdu reading-comprehension questions for Taleemabad. He has 40 generated questions in a spreadsheet and one column headed 'Quality (1-5)'. He grades all 40 in an afternoon. Then he hands the same 40 to his teammate to double-check, and the two score sheets come back different on 17 of the 40 rows — including question #12, which Ali gave a 4 and his teammate gave a 2.
research.friction: Ali cannot defend a single number. Sitting with question #12 open — a question asking a 9-year-old to 'analyse the author's tone' — he says '4, it reads well.' His teammate says '2, a Grade 4 child cannot answer that.' They are both right, because they were never grading the same thing: Ali was scoring fluency of the Urdu, his teammate was scoring age-appropriateness. Nothing in the spreadsheet said which one 'Quality' meant. Worse, when Ali re-grades ten rows the next morning to settle it, he changes three of his own scores. The 40 numbers are unusable — he cannot tell the model team what to fix, because 'raise the average from 3.1 to 4' names no defect.
research.fix: Ali stops scoring and instead writes down, before looking at any question, the four things he was actually checking all along, one line each, each answerable yes/no by someone reading only that line: (1) the question can be answered using only the passage above it; (2) the vocabulary is within the Grade 4 Urdu word list; (3) exactly one of the four options is correct; (4) the question asks for recall or inference, not literary analysis. Then he re-grades all 40 as four checkboxes per row instead of one number. Question #12 now reads: passage-answerable YES, vocabulary YES, one-correct-option YES, recall-or-inference NO — 3 of 4, and the failing box is named. He and his teammate re-grade independently and now agree on 38 of 40; the 2 they still disagree on are both on criterion 2, which sends them to look up what the Grade 4 word list actually contains.
research.failure_mode: The rubric still breaks if a criterion is not independently checkable. Ali's first draft of criterion 4 read 'the question is at the right cognitive level' — which is the same fog as 'quality', just wearing a lab coat. Four boxes of vagueness is worse than one honest number, because the checkboxes make it LOOK measured. The other way it breaks: a criterion that two graders can only agree on by talking to each other. If Ali's teammate has to ask 'what did you mean by right level?', that line is not a criterion yet, it is a conversation. Test each line by handing it to someone cold and seeing whether they can answer without asking a question back.
research.payoff: Ali can now hand the model team a defect report instead of an average: '31 of 40 questions fail criterion 4 — the model keeps asking for literary analysis.' That is one prompt change, retestable against the same four boxes tomorrow. He can also hand the rubric to a second grader, or to a model grader, and get scores he can compare — because the rubric, not the person, is doing the judging.
misconceptions: 'A rubric is just a scoring scale (1-5, or 1-10).' No — the scale is the least important part. A rubric is the list of named checks; the number is what falls out of them
'A more detailed rubric is a better rubric.' No — 12 criteria that nobody applies consistently is worse than 4 that everyone does. Independently checkable beats comprehensive

'I know what I mean by good quality, so writing it down is bureaucracy.' The point is not that Ali does not know — it is that his knowledge is not transferable, not repeatable, and not comparable across two graders or two weeks
'If two graders disagree, the rubric failed.' The opposite: a rubric that surfaces disagreement on a named criterion has done its job. Silent agreement on a vague number is the failure
'Rubrics are for human graders; a model judge does not need one.' A model judge needs it more — a rubric is the only thing standing between you and a model that scores on vibes at scale

research.topic: What a rubric actually does in an eval — turning a vague quality judgement into a fixed set of observable checks that different graders apply the same way
research.slo: The learner can take a vague quality standard ("is this answer good?") and rewrite it as a rubric of observable, independently-checkable criteria that two different graders would score identically.
research.audience: Content and product people at Taleemabad who are starting to evaluate AI outputs. They have seen an eval run and know an eval means checking outputs against expectations (evals-01 to evals-04). They have never written a rubric and currently judge outputs by gut feel. No coding assumed.
key_points: A rubric is not a scoring form or a grade — it is the written definition of what "good" means for one specific task, in terms a second person could apply without asking you what you meant.
Each criterion must be observable in the output itself: you can point at the text and say yes or no. "Correct grade level" is observable; "feels appropriate" is not.
A rubric splits one blurry judgement into a few independent checks, so a failing output tells you WHICH part failed, not just that it scored low.
The rubric's real job is agreement: the test of a rubric is that two graders scoring the same output land on the same result — not that the score looks impressive.

This video covers what a rubric does and why criteria must be observable and independent; HOW to write and word the criteria line by line is the next video (evals-05), and this SLO only needs the "what it does" half.
research.ali_scenario: Ali is checking an AI assistant that writes Grade 4 Urdu reading-comprehension questions from a story passage. He generates 20 questions from the same passage about a boy who loses his goat, and has to decide which ones are usable in a real worksheet.
research.friction: Ali reads each of the 20 questions and marks them out of 5 by feel — he gives question 3 a 4, question 7 a 2, and so on, ending with an average of 3.4. Then Sara on his team grades the same 20 with the same 0–5 scale and averages 2.1. Neither can explain the gap: Ali counted a two-part question as fine because a teacher could split it, Sara marked it down because it confuses a nine-year-old. When Ali asks the AI to improve, he can only say "make them better," the next batch scores 3.6, and he cannot tell whether anything actually improved or he was just in a better mood on Tuesday.
research.fix: Ali stops scoring the whole question and writes down four things he can literally point at in the text: (1) the answer appears in the passage, not from outside knowledge; (2) it asks exactly one thing — no "and" joining two questions; (3) every word is on the Grade 4 vocabulary list; (4) it is not answerable with just yes or no. He re-grades the 20 questions as four yes/no checks each instead of one gut number. Sara grades the same 20 with the same four checks. They now agree on 19 of 20, and the one they disagree on exposes a criterion that was still vague — "Grade 4 vocabulary" — which Ali pins to a specific word list. The counts also tell him where the model is actually weak: 15 of 20 pass the passage-grounding check, but only 8 pass the one-thing check, so he fixes the prompt for compound questions specifically.
research.failure_mode: Ali gets excited and stretches the rubric to eleven criteria, several of them overlapping ("single question," "not compound," "clear") and one still subjective ("engaging for children"). Grading 20 outputs now takes an hour, and the overlapping criteria triple-punish the same flaw so one compound question drops three checks and looks like a catastrophe, while "engaging" quietly reintroduces the Ali-vs-Sara disagreement he just eliminated. A rubric with more criteria is not a better rubric — every criterion has to be observable and non-overlapping, or it adds noise instead of signal.
research.payoff: Ali can now hand the four checks to anyone on the team — or to an automated grader — and get the same verdict he would have given himself, and he can say precisely what to fix: not "make them better" but "8 of 20 ask two things at once." His before/after comparisons become real evidence instead of a mood, because the standard stopped living in his head and started living on paper.
misconceptions: That a rubric is the numeric score or the star rating — the number is the output; the rubric is the definition of what earns it.
That a rubric is only for grading humans, like a teacher's marking sheet, and has nothing to do with testing an AI system.
That a rubric must be long and exhaustive to be rigorous — four sharp observable checks beat twenty vague ones.
That criteria like "clear," "helpful," or "high quality" are usable criteria; they are just the original vague judgement wearing a rubric's clothes.
That once a rubric is written it is fixed forever — disagreement between graders is the signal that a criterion needs sharpening, not that a grader is wrong.

research.topic: AI in 2030 — why the bottleneck moves from model capability to verification of AI output
research.slo: Given an AI system that is more capable than the human reviewing it, the learner can explain why the reviewer's job shifts from producing work to designing checks that catch wrong work, and can name one check that survives an AI that is confidently wrong.
research.audience: Taleemabad L&D and product people, and teachers-turned-content-builders, who already use AI assistants day to day and have heard '2030 predictions' talk. They know prompting; they have never had to verify output they could not personally have produced.
key_points: This video teaches ONE concept: verification becomes the scarce skill when the AI is faster and broader than you. The other candidate concept in 'AI in 2030' — capability forecasting / timelines — is deliberately not taught, because the SLO is about what the learner DOES, not about predicting dates.
By 2030 the cheap thing is production of plausible work; the expensive thing is knowing whether that work is right. Cost curves invert what a knowledge worker's day looks like.
'It reads well' is not a check. Plausibility is exactly what a strong model optimises, so fluency carries zero information about correctness.
A real check is one the AI cannot satisfy by writing better prose: it hits ground truth outside the AI's output — a source you open, a number you recompute, a sample you spot-inspect.
You cannot verify everything, so you verify where being wrong is most costly and hardest to detect later — that choice is the actual skill.
Checks must be decided BEFORE you see the output; deciding after means you grade against what you were handed.
research.ali_scenario: Ali, a curriculum lead at Taleemabad in 2030, is handed one task with a Friday deadline: publish a Grade 5 maths practice set of 120 questions for the new term. His AI assistant generates all 120 questions with answer keys, worked solutions, difficulty tags and Urdu translations in about 40 seconds. He has roughly two hours before he has to ship. 120 items, 2 hours — about one minute per item if he tried to do all of them, which he cannot.
research.friction: Ali does what feels responsible: he starts reading the questions from the top. They are excellent — clean wording, sensible difficulty ramp, tidy Urdu. He reads 30, finds nothing wrong, feels the deadline, and ships all 120 on the strength of 'the ones I read were fine.' Two weeks later a teacher reports that question 87 asks for the area of a rectangle but the answer key gives the perimeter, and question 103's Urdu translation says 'subtract' where the English says 'divide.' Both read perfectly. Ali's reading pass could never have caught them, because he was checking whether the questions sounded like good questions — the one thing the model was guaranteed to get right. He had spent his two hours confirming fluency and had no evidence at all about correctness.
research.fix: Before opening the output, Ali writes down what could be wrong and how he would know, then spends his two hours only on those. He picks three checks. One: recompute — he solves 12 items himself, chosen not at random but 12 where the answer is a number he can recheck in ten seconds, and compares to the key; question 87's mismatch surfaces on item four. Two: cross-language diff — he has the AI back-translate all 40 Urdu items to English and he scans only for verbs that changed, which catches 103 in under a minute. Three: distribution — he counts how many items land in each difficulty tag and finds 71 of 120 tagged 'medium', a shape no real practice set has. Each check touches ground truth the AI's writing cannot fake: arithmetic he redid, a word-level mismatch between two versions, a count. He ships with 3 known defects fixed and a note on what he did and did not check.
research.failure_mode: The checks quietly stop being checks. Ali reuses the same three every term, the AI's next version learns to produce clean back-translations and a pretty difficulty histogram, and now his checks pass on output he has not actually verified — he is measuring the things that got easy while the errors moved to pedagogy, to whether a question is worth asking at all. Worse, he starts letting the AI run the checks and report 'all clear', which makes the checker and the thing being checked the same system. A check only works while it hits something outside the model's output and while it still sometimes fails; a check that never fails has become a ritual, and Ali has to keep asking what a wrong item would look like NOW, not last term.
research.payoff: Ali can now ship work he did not personally produce and cannot personally reproduce, and still say honestly what he knows about it — 'I recomputed 12, I diffed the translations, I checked the difficulty spread; I did not check pedagogical value.' That sentence is what makes him useful in 2030. He is no longer competing with the AI on output speed, a race he loses; he is doing the part it cannot do for itself — deciding what would count as wrong, and going and looking. It also scales: 1,200 items would not take ten times longer, because checks are chosen by risk, not by volume.
misconceptions: 'When the models get good enough in 2030, verification stops mattering.' It matters more — you verify precisely because you can no longer tell by looking, and the volume you're accountable for goes up.
'Spot-checking means reading a random sample.' Reading is not checking. A sample you only read tells you the output is fluent, which you already knew.
'The AI can check its own work if I ask it to.' It can, and it will agree with itself. A check needs a source of truth the generating system does not control.
'If I can't review all of it, reviewing some of it is meaningless.' Targeted partial checks with a stated scope are the working method; unbounded reading is what's meaningless.
'2030 AI means the job disappears.' The producing part shrinks; the deciding-what-good-means part grows, and it is the part nobody has automated.

reasons: One protagonist named Ali, one running scenario (a Grade Five maths practice set) followed from friction through payoff — no list of separate domain examples.
Exactly one concept: verification is the scarce skill, and a real check must be something plausible-sounding output cannot pass and the model cannot run on itself.

Arc runs in order: friction (01-08 shipped on a read-through and an error came back), fix (11-12 write the checks before opening the output), structure (13-16 the three checks), failure mode (17-18 the AI running its own checks), payoff (19-22).
All 22 beats are within the 16-22 house range; every vo is a single sentence; no title cards.
Every 'ali' beat (01, 05, 10) has a single subject with props detached and floating; every multi-object or second-person composition is correctly 'scene'.

No art prompt requests text, letters, numbers, labels or signage; all specify flat 2D vector on plain cream with no ground, shadow, desk, scenery or dark fill; Ali is described identically in all 16 art prompts.
Mandatory in-video QUESTION -> REVEAL is present: beat 17 asks with a quiz-style checks card, beat 18 reveals.
Info-card data is short and within template shape; the gauge on 16 carries value 71 against max 120 with a good marker at 40, matching the spoken line.
Remaining fixes are minor only — wording length on a few beats and one holdAfter nicety. None block production.

fixes.problem: The question beat carries the quiz content but the script does not show a `holdAfter` on it, so the reveal may land before the viewer has answered.
fixes.suggested: Add `"holdAfter": 3` (or the house default) to beat 17 so the four options stay on screen before beat 18 reveals 'None of them'.

fixes.problem: The sentence is the longest in the script (two clauses plus a timing claim) and may feel rushed at the measured pace.
fixes.suggested: Trim to 'He back-translates the Urdu and scans only for verbs that changed, catching one in under a minute.'

fixes.problem: The em-dash mid-sentence can read as a hard stop in TTS.
fixes.suggested: Replace the dash with a comma: 'You are not competing with the machine on output, you are deciding what would count as wrong and going to look.'

fixes.problem: The statement card's `hi` is '120' while the card text spells the number as a numeral too, so the highlight adds little emphasis.
fixes.suggested: Set `hi` to 'Two hours' so the highlight lands on the scarce resource rather than repeating the count.

fixes.problem: The vo is slightly abstract ('information the model could never have handed him') right after a concrete beat, which softens the moment.
fixes.suggested: Consider 'What that colleague pushes back on is something the model was never in a position to tell him.'

fixes.problem: Beat 17 uses `tpl: "checks"` for the quiz; the house pattern for the interactive question is the `quiz` template.
fixes.suggested: Switch to `"tpl": "quiz"` with the same four options if the quiz template is available, so the question renders in the established QUESTION -> REVEAL styling.
